messages.author: 1557f895f706963e
messages.subject: ggplot2 and memory-efficient data structures
parts: As far as I know, ggplot2 can use data frames, but not matrices. This is a problem because data frames can be extremely memory inefficient, as I show here. It would be really nice if future releases of ggplot2 could use matrices and their dimnames attributes. Is anyone currently working on this?

messages.author: 373beb702917b8b5
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 and memory-efficient data structures
parts:
Hi Will,

The current situation is not really as bad as you suggest in your blog
post. If you have huge data, chances are good that you want to
summarize it in some way prior to plotting; in your blog post example
you summarize by counting the number of observations in bins. There is
no reason that this has to be done inside a ggplot() call. To continue
your example:


## summarize the data
library(plyr)

a.hist <- adply(a.array, .(2, 3, 4),
function(x) {
as.data.frame(hist(x, plot=FALSE)[c("mids", "counts")])
})

## little wasted space, as the summary is quite small
print(object.size(a.hist), units = "Kb")

## plot the pre-summarized data
ggplot(a.hist, aes(x=mids, y=counts)) +
geom_histogram(aes(fill=X1, color=X1),
alpha=0.5,
position="identity",
stat="identity") +
facet_grid(X2 ~ X3)

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 and memory-efficient data structures
parts: Thanks for the helpful preprocessing code. This is certainly the ideal thing to do for one-dimensional histograms. However, I still think it would be nice if ggplot2 took care of summarization under the hood at the matrix level, even if it just involves a single call to adply. After all, preprocessing for other plots can be more complicated. For example, I often use hexagonal bins to reduce the size of my scatterplots, and writing my own code to calculate bins and bin frequencies seems like reinventing the wheel.

On 13-10-02 05:32 PM, Will L wrote:
>

> Thanks for the helpful preprocessing code. This is certainly the ideal
> thing to do for one-dimensional histograms. However, I still think it would
> be nice if ggplot2 took care of summarization under the hood at the matrix
> level, even if it just involves a single call to adply. After all,
> preprocessing for other plots can be more complicated. For example, I often
> use hexagonal bins to reduce the size of my scatterplots, and writing my
> own code to calculate bins and bin frequencies seems like reinventing the
> wheel.

It certainly would be nice, but I think it would actually amount to
re-engineering a significant fraction of the package; the convenience of
assuming that everything is already in long format is what makes ggplot
(in its current form) so flexible. You might want to check out the
'bigvis' package: https://github.com/hadley/bigvis , which I think comes
very close to addressing your concerns, but keep in mind that HW is a
Really Really Really Busy Guy with more good ideas than he has time for:
https://github.com/hadley?tab=contributions&period=monthly (among other
things, he is working on the `dplyr` package to make data manipulation
faster too ...)

I would quibble slightly, by the way, with your characterization of
the memory problems. It's not really "data frames vs. matrices", nor
storing extra copies of strings -- it's really "wide" or
"multidimensional" vs "long" ...

cheers
Ben Bolker

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 and memory-efficient data structures
parts:
> It certainly would be nice, but I think it would actually amount to
> re-engineering a significant fraction of the package; the convenience of
> assuming that everything is already in long format is what makes ggplot
> (in its current form) so flexible. You might want to check out the
> 'bigvis' package: https://github.com/hadley/bigvis , which I think comes
> very close to addressing your concerns, but keep in mind that HW is a
> Really Really Really Busy Guy with more good ideas than he has time for:
> https://github.com/hadley?tab=contributions&period=monthly (among other
> things, he is working on the `dplyr` package to make data manipulation
> faster too ...)

Yes, I am busy :) Currently, you do want to do as much processing
outside of ggplot2 as possible because the fundamental design of
ggplot2 is very computationally inefficient (but it is cognitively
efficient which is what I was aiming for, because I think that's
usually the bigger bottleneck). A design goal for the next iteration
of ggplot2 is to support more types of input data, but the big
advantage of standard formats (however inefficient) is that you have a
standard way of working with them.

See the conclusion of http://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.html for
more on this theme.

> I would quibble slightly, by the way, with your characterization of
> the memory problems. It's not really "data frames vs. matrices", nor
> storing extra copies of strings -- it's really "wide" or
> "multidimensional" vs "long" ...

Also, the strings aren't stored as inefficiently as you might think

x <- "banana"
y <- rep(x, 1e5)

object.size(x)
object.size(y) / 1e5

Hadley

--
Chief Scientist, RStudio
http://had.co.nz/
